newsitem.title: USA: Bill seeks to repeal Florida tobacco law.
newsitem.headline: Bill seeks to repeal Florida tobacco law.

text.p: A Florida state senator Thursday unveiled a proposal to repeal the 1994 law Florida is using to sue tobacco companies for more than $1 billion spent treating smoking-related illnesses.

Sen. Charles Williams, D-Tallahassee, announced the filing of the repealer at a news conference, saying the 1994 measure strips defendants of traditional legal defenses and sets up a two-tiered system of justice for tobacco companies.
"Florida is sending a mixed message to the American business community," Williams said in a statement. "We want your business, jobs and taxes, but we may sue you later if we don't like you."

The law in question was passed during the last days of the 1994 state legislative session. Targeted at the tobacco industry, the measure allows Florida to use statistical data to prove its case that tobacco-related illnesses have cost it more than $1.4 billion since 1994.
The law also prevents cigarette makers from using the traditional defense of comparative negligence, permitted to other defendants in product liability cases.
Opponents of the measure tried and failed to repeal the law last year, after Gov. Lawton Chiles, a Democrat who has crusaded against tobacco companies, secured enough votes keep the law in place.
Williams said Thursday it was too early to tell if he had the votes to pass the measure in the Senate. No House version has been filed.

Florida is using the 1994 law to sue the industry over Medicaid payments made by the state to pay for smoking related illnesses. In 1996, the Florida Supreme Court upheld key provisions of the law. A civil lawsuit filed in a West Palm Beach circuit court, is scheduled to go to trial in August.
